etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/napo/ → /nafo/ → /nawo/ → /nao/
From Old Japanese.
The okurigana spelling 尚(な)お (nao), or more accurately its historical kana usage counterpart 尚(な)ほ (nafo), used to be very common and the de facto standard, but has become obsolete since the introduction of modern kana usage in 1946. Compare 古(いにしえ) (inishie) and its historically common spelling 古(いにし)へ (inisife).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compare verbs 直(なお)る (naoru, “to be repaired”), 直(なお)す (naosu, “to fix, to repair”), 治(なお)る (naoru, “to heal”), and 治(なお)す (naosu, “to cure, to heal”), all cognates with a common thread of becoming or making something become normal, ordinary, or right again.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 日 (“Japan”) + 中 (“China”) or blend of 日本 (Nihon, Nippon, “Japan”) + 中国 (Chūgoku, “China”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Sinitic 日中. Date of borrowing unknown.
